title: Shift-Left Security: SAST/DAST & Dependency Scanning
summary: Push security into the developer workflow: SAST/DAST/IAST lenses, dependency scanning, pipeline gates with real teeth, Trivy image scanning in CI, governed triage, and the OWASP coverage map panels expect.
objectives: Distinguish SAST, DAST, and IAST and place each correctly in the pipeline
Scan dependencies with npm audit, pip-audit, and related SCA tooling
Design pipeline security gates with thresholds and speed-appropriate placement
Scan container images with Trivy in CI and remediate via the base-first ladder
Run governed triage with allowlists, metrics, and an OWASP coverage map

notes.title: SAST, DAST, and IAST: Three Different Lenses
notes.body: Shift-left means finding vulnerabilities where they are cheapest to fix — in the developer's workflow, not in production. Three techniques cover three lenses. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads source code without running it: it finds SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, and insecure crypto before the code ever executes. Tools: Semgrep (semgrep scan --config auto), Bandit for Python (bandit -r src/), CodeQL. DAST (Dynamic AST) attacks the running application: OWASP ZAP spiders the site and fires payloads at it, finding what static analysis cannot — authentication flaws, server misconfigurations, runtime injection. IAST (Interactive AST) instruments the running app (an agent inside the JVM/CLR) and watches real execution, combining code context with runtime proof. Worked example: where does each catch a SQL injection? SAST flags the string-concatenated query at commit time; DAST proves it by injecting ' OR '1'='1 into the live login form in staging; IAST watches the test suite execute the vulnerable path and reports the exact tainted-data flow. The panel point: SAST is fast and early but noisy; DAST is proof but late and needs a running environment; IAST is precise but requires instrumentation. Mature pipelines run SAST on every PR, DAST nightly against staging, IAST in integration tests.

notes.title: Dependency (SCA) Scanning: Your Code Is 10% Yours
notes.body: Modern applications are overwhelmingly third-party code — frameworks, transitive dependencies, native packages — and vulnerabilities arrive through them (the supply-chain reality behind every 'critical CVE in a library you never chose'). SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scans your dependency manifests and lockfiles against vulnerability databases. The commands are built into your toolchain: npm audit (and npm audit fix, carefully), pip-audit -r requirements.txt for Python, dotnet list package --vulnerable, cargo audit, go list with govulncheck. The pipeline step fails the build on critical/high CVEs, with an allowlist for accepted risks that carries an expiry date and an owner — never a permanent ignore. Worked example: pip-audit reports CVE-2024-XXXX critical in requests 2.28.0 via requirements.txt. Solution: (1) confirm exploitability — is the vulnerable code path reachable? (2) upgrade to the patched 2.32.x and run the test suite; (3) if the upgrade breaks, evaluate the backported patch or isolate the call path, and only then add a time-boxed exception with owner and review date. The trap: npm audit fix blindly upgrading majors and breaking the build the night before release — pin versions (the M50 requirements.txt lesson), review the diff, and let CI prove the upgrade.

notes.title: Pipeline Security Gates: Fail the Build, Not the Audit
notes.body: A security gate is a pipeline stage that blocks promotion when risk exceeds policy: SAST findings above threshold, critical CVEs in dependencies, container image vulnerabilities, or leaked secrets. Gate design matters more than gate existence. Thresholds: fail on critical always; fail on high unless allowlisted with expiry; warn on medium. Placement: fast checks (SAST, SCA, secret scan) on every pull request where the developer can fix in minutes; slow checks (full DAST, image scan of the final artifact) on merge to main before staging deploy. Worked example: a Jenkins/GitHub Actions stage after unit tests: run trivy on the built image, semgrep on the diff, pip-audit on requirements. If any critical appears, the stage fails, the PR is blocked, and the finding links to the exact line and the fix guidance. Solution review: the developer fixes it in the PR in ten minutes; the alternative — found in a quarterly audit — costs a ticket, a meeting, and a hotfix. The anti-pattern is the advisory-only gate that everyone ignores: a gate that never blocks is a dashboard, not a control. Start strict on new code (block), advisory on legacy (ratchet), and tighten the ratchet quarterly.

notes.title: Container Image Scanning in CI with Trivy
notes.body: Container images bundle an OS userland plus your app, so they inherit every CVE in both. Scanning the final image in CI — after build, before push — is the choke point: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:pr-123 fails the pipeline on high/critical findings. Scan the base image separately and regularly, because base CVEs arrive without any code change on your part. The remediation ladder: (1) rebuild on a patched base (use minimal bases — distroless or alpine — to shrink the CVE surface); (2) update the application dependencies; (3) only then, allowlist a specific CVE with expiry when it is provably unreachable. Worked example: trivy flags CRITICAL CVE-2024-YYYY in openssl inside your python:3.11 base. Solution: check for python:3.11-slim patched tag or the distroless variant, rebuild, rescan — the finding should clear; if the patch is not yet released, document the exposure window, add a 14-day allowlist with owner, and set a calendar reminder, not a permanent ignore. The M-series callback: this is the Dockerfile lesson made operational — multi-stage builds and minimal bases from the Docker module are what make these scans passable in the first place.

notes.title: Triaging Findings: Signal, Noise, and the Allowlist
notes.body: Scanners produce findings; engineers produce judgments. Triage sorts every finding into: true positive and exploitable (fix now), true positive but unreachable (allowlist with expiry and justification), false positive (suppress with reason, revisit on tool upgrade), and duplicate (dedupe to the root cause). The allowlist is a governed document, not a junk drawer: each entry has the CVE/finding ID, why it is accepted (unreachable path, compensating control), an owner, and an expiry date — expired entries re-alert automatically. Metrics keep the program honest: mean time to remediate criticals, percentage of findings allowlisted (a rising share means the gate is being bypassed culturally), and scanner coverage (what percentage of repos run the gates). Worked example: SAST flags 'hardcoded password' on test fixtures using 'password123' against a local test database. Solution: true positive pattern, unreachable in production — but the right fix is not an allowlist, it is moving the fixture to a secrets-free test helper; allowlist only when the code cannot be made clean. The panel point: 'How do you handle false positives?' is a culture question — the answer is a governed triage process with expiry, not 'we ignore the scanner.'

notes.title: Mapping to OWASP: What the Scanners Are Hunting
notes.body: The OWASP Top 10 is the shared vocabulary for what all this tooling hunts: injection (SAST + DAST), broken access control (DAST + manual review), cryptographic failures (SAST flags weak algorithms), vulnerable components (SCA), security misconfiguration (DAST + image scan), and the rest. Each pipeline gate maps to categories: SAST covers injection and crypto; SCA covers vulnerable components; DAST covers access control, misconfiguration, and auth failures; image scanning covers the platform layer beneath the app. Worked example: map a pipeline to the Top 10 for a panel. Solution: 'PR gates — Semgrep (injection, crypto), pip-audit/npm audit (vulnerable components), gitleaks (secrets, feeding M48); merge gates — Trivy image scan (misconfiguration, known OS CVEs); nightly — ZAP baseline against staging (access control, auth, misconfiguration). Every Top 10 category has at least one automated check, and the allowlist governs the exceptions.' The interview move: never recite the Top 10 as trivia — narrate it as your pipeline's coverage map. That turns a memorization question into an architecture answer, which is exactly what senior panels reward.

quiz.q: Where does SAST catch a SQL injection, and where does DAST prove it?
choices: SAST at commit time flags the concatenated query; DAST proves it by injecting into the live staging login form
quiz.explain: SAST sees the code pattern early; DAST demonstrates exploitability against the running app. IAST would trace the tainted flow during tests.

quiz.q: pip-audit reports a critical CVE in requests 2.28.0. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Confirm exploitability -> upgrade to patched version and run tests -> time-boxed exception only if upgrade is impossible
quiz.explain: Verify reachability, upgrade and prove with CI, and only then allowlist with owner and expiry. Blind auto-fix can break the build.

choices: Fast checks (SAST/SCA/secret scan) per PR; slow checks (full DAST, final image scan) on merge
All security testing once a year
quiz.explain: Speed-appropriate placement: PR gates give ten-minute fixes; merge gates protect staging; nightly DAST covers depth.

quiz.q: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:pr-123 exits 1. What happened?
choices: The image contains HIGH or CRITICAL findings, so the pipeline stage fails and the PR is blocked
quiz.explain: --exit-code 1 turns findings into a gate failure — the choke point between build and push.

quiz.q: Trivy flags a critical OpenSSL CVE in your python:3.11 base. First remediation step?
choices: Rebuild on a patched/minimal base (slim or distroless) and rescan
quiz.explain: The remediation ladder starts with the base: patched minimal bases clear whole CVE classes. Allowlisting is the last resort, time-boxed.

quiz.q: SAST flags 'hardcoded password' in test fixtures using password123 against a local test DB. Best handling?
choices: Fix the code: move fixtures to a secrets-free helper; allowlist only what cannot be made clean
quiz.explain: Triage prefers fixing over allowlisting; the allowlist is for provably unreachable findings, not for cleanable code.

quiz.q: A gate that reports findings but never blocks is:
choices: A dashboard, not a control — start strict on new code, advisory on legacy with a quarterly ratchet
quiz.explain: Controls must control. The ratchet pattern (block new, advisory legacy, tighten quarterly) makes strictness adoptable.

quiz.q: Which Top 10 category does the SCA gate cover?
quiz.explain: SCA exists for the components category — npm audit/pip-audit on every PR is its operational form.

quiz.q: Mean time to remediate criticals is rising and allowlist share is climbing. What does this indicate?
choices: Cultural bypass: findings are being deferred rather than fixed — tighten ownership and review the allowlist
quiz.explain: Rising allowlist share with slowing remediation means the gate is being routed around. Metrics exist to catch exactly this.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: shift-left gates on a real pipeline
handsOnLab.brief: You will wire SAST, SCA, secret scanning, and Trivy image gates into a CI pipeline for a sample app, watch them catch planted vulnerabilities, triage the findings, and prove the allowlist discipline.
steps: Clone the sample app (Python Flask + Dockerfile) and plant three issues: a bandit-flaggable subprocess call, an outdated requests version in requirements.txt, and a fake AWS key in a comment.
Add the PR-gate job: bandit -r src/ with exit-code fail, semgrep scan --config auto, pip-audit -r requirements.txt, and gitleaks detect --no-git (or equivalent secret scan).
Run the pipeline and record all three findings; verify the build fails (non-zero exit).
Triage each: fix the subprocess call properly, upgrade requests and let tests prove it, remove the fake key and rotate the pattern.
Rebuild the Docker image with a minimal base (python:3.11-slim) and multi-stage build; run trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 on it.
Record the Trivy findings; remediate by base/dependency updates; for one provably-unreachable finding, create an allowlist entry with ID, justification, owner, and 14-day expiry.
Add the merge gate: full Trivy scan of the final image before push; confirm a critical blocks the push.
Run zap-baseline.py -t against a local staging deploy of the app; record the DAST findings and map each to an OWASP Top 10 category.
Write the coverage map: which gate covers which Top 10 categories, in a one-page table.
Measure: time from finding to fix for each planted issue; note which gate caught it fastest.
Expire-test: backdate the allowlist expiry and confirm the pipeline re-alerts.
Document the ratchet plan: which gates block today, which are advisory on legacy repos, and the quarterly tightening schedule.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A CI pipeline with four working gates, triaged findings with a governed allowlist, a ZAP baseline report, and an OWASP coverage map.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All planted issues are caught and fixed; the pipeline fails on a new critical; the allowlist entry re-alerts after expiry; the coverage map covers every Top 10 category.

mockTask.q: Your new SAST gate flags 200 findings on a legacy repo on day one, and developers demand it be turned off. What do you do?
choices: Make it advisory on legacy code with a quarterly ratchet, but keep it blocking on new code — and triage the 200 into fix/allowlist-with-expiry buckets with owners
mockTask.explain: Day-one blocking on legacy debt kills adoption; advisory-with-ratchet preserves the control while the backlog is triaged. New code stays strict so debt stops growing, and every legacy finding gets an owner and an expiry — not a permanent pass.
